findings.headline: Transport operations audit found six operational categories unsatisfactory; remediation due July 2026
findings.detail: A Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency registered auditor reviewed transport operations in March 2026 against 65 criteria. Six categories were classified as unsatisfactory, covering CO2 emissions, driver eye tests, and vehicle safety. All remedial actions are scheduled for completion by 31 July 2026.
findings.matters: Operational compliance failures in transport operations represent control weaknesses and potential licence liability. Tight remediation timelines suggest urgent issues that could affect service continuity.
findings.figures: 65 criteria examined; 6 categories rated unsatisfactory; deadline 31 July 2026
findings.quote: A Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency registered auditor undertook a review of transport operations in March 2026. The review examined 65 separate criteria and classified 6 categories as 'unsatisfactory'.

findings.headline: Social Housing Regulator gave C2 rating (below target C1), requiring improvement in tenant engagement and repairs
findings.detail: A mock inspection by the Regulator of Social Housing in 2025/26 gave a C2 rating on a scale where C1 is highest. The council is pursuing a service improvement programme with focus on tenant engagement and repairs to achieve the target C1 rating.
findings.matters: A C2 regulatory rating indicates the council is not fully meeting regulatory expectations in housing management and service delivery. This directly reflects on the quality and compliance of housing operations.
findings.figures: Rating scale C1 (highest) to C4; council achieved C2
findings.quote: The council commissioned a mock inspection by the Regulator of Social Housing during 2025/26; this inspection gave the council a 'C2' rating.

findings.headline: Information governance reporting has fallen behind due to resourcing constraints, with backlog extending into 2026/27
findings.detail: The mandatory annual Information Governance Report was not produced for 2024/25 and is scheduled for 2026/27 'resources permitting'. This creates a compliance gap in mandatory reporting on data protection, information governance, data breaches, and Freedom of Information performance.
findings.matters: Information governance is a statutory reporting requirement. Persistent resourcing gaps preventing compliance reports suggest staff constraints and inability to adequately manage data protection and compliance risks.
findings.figures: Reports delayed: 2024/25 not produced; 2025/26 deferred to 2026/27
findings.quote: No report was produced for 24/25 due to resourcing issues. The 25/26 outturn position will be presented to Committee during the 26/27 year, again resources permitting.

findings.headline: Internal Audit opinion is moderate, not substantial, indicating control weaknesses persist
findings.detail: Internal Audit raised the annual opinion from 'limited' in the prior year to 'moderate' in 2025/26, based on 11 completed audits: 2 rated substantial, 5 moderate, 3 limited, and 1 with no assurance. While 90 historic recommendations were closed, the ongoing mix of audit ratings shows control issues remain.
findings.matters: A moderate audit opinion means the council's internal controls are not fully robust. Lenders require substantial or unqualified audit opinions as evidence of financial control effectiveness.
findings.figures: 11 internal audits completed: 2 substantial, 5 moderate, 3 limited, 1 no assurance; 90 prior-year recommendations closed
findings.quote: Internal Audit considers that corporate governance, risk management and internal control processes have improved in 2025/26, sufficiently to raise the overall opinion from 'limited' to 'moderate'.

findings.headline: Housing maintenance service failed to external contractor and was replaced with in-house provision within 12 months
findings.detail: The council ended its joint venture with Norse Group (UNSL) on 31 March 2025 and contracted with Axis Europe from 1 April 2025. However, Axis encountered 'operational, performance, and delivery challenges' that led to early termination. The council then implemented an in-house maintenance service from 1 April 2026. This represents two major service model changes in 12 months and suggests either unexpected costs or service quality issues from the contracted provider.
findings.matters: Service delivery disruption and rapid strategy reversal indicate procurement or contract management issues that could result in unexpected financial exposure and operational risk to housing services.
findings.figures: Three transitions in 12 months: UNSL ceased 31 March 2025; Axis Europe from 1 April 2025; in-house from 1 April 2026
findings.quote: Following the mobilisation of the Axis contract, we encountered several operational, performance, and delivery challenges. These issues ultimately led to the early cessation of the contract and the decision to implement an In-House Maintenance Service, which went live on 1 April 2026.

findings.headline: Commercial portfolio valuation has declined against purchase price; Skyway House lost £5.5m and Amazon lost £6.75m since acquisition
findings.detail: Asset valuations as at 30 September 2025 show material declines. Skyway House (paid £20m, valued £14.5m), Amazon Gloucester (paid £42.7m, valued £35.95m), and others show similar patterns. The non-CRP portfolio shows £186.8m cost against £169.65m valuation (9% loss overall). Only the disputed Aspire valuation at £110.35m supports the total portfolio claim of £280m.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand the trend in asset values and whether further decline is expected; this affects the security available against the £238.6m borrowing position
findings.figures: Portfolio cost £275.6m valued at £280m; non-CRP assets £186.8m cost vs £169.65m valuation; individual declines: Skyway £5.5m, Amazon £6.75m, others material
findings.quote: Whilst asset values have declined, the rental income has increased through rent reviews.

findings.headline: Council is committing £68.6m to Chesterford Research Park expansion through 2031 despite rule constraints and inability to exit
findings.detail: Despite being unable to sell the 50% stake and facing a changed regulatory environment, the council is committed to major capital at the park: £40m for new buildings, £5.1m for refurbishment, £13.5m for end-of-lease refurbishment by 2031. Para 22 forecasts annual contributions of £4-12.6m. No payment is due on the largest loans until April 2026-2027, creating a cliff.
findings.matters: Lenders need to assess whether the council can sustain this level of capital commitment given stated budget shortfalls; construction cost inflation or tenant issues could force additional unplanned borrowing
findings.figures: £68.6m total: New Building 1 £40m, Building 500 £10m, Building 900 refurbishment £5.1m, other lease-end refurbishment £13.5m
findings.quote: The joint venture 5 year business plan for Chesterford Research Park sets out ambitions for two new builds as well as specific refurbishment of Building 900. Over the lifetime of the plan there will also be a number of other units reaching end of lease and requiring refurbishment, accordingly a contribution of £1,500,000 has been built into the 2026/27 financial year and £3,000,000 each year thereafter.

findings.headline: CIPFA rule changes force the council to hold all assets long-term instead of the planned sell-and-refresh strategy
findings.detail: The original plan was to sell assets after holding them, reinvest proceeds, and avoid asset aging. This is no longer possible: para 39 states 'It will not now be possible to sell assets and buy new, the council will need to retain some or all of the assets for the longer term.' This lock-in increases refurbishment risk as assets age through lease cycles.
findings.matters: Lenders need to know the portfolio is becoming progressively older with rising end-of-lease costs; the council is building a £500k annual reserve but holds only £6m total against £275.6m in assets
findings.figures: £275.6m portfolio; £6m Commercial Asset Reserve at end 2025/26; £500k annual contributions; major refurbishment costs forecast £1.5m-£3m annually from 2027
findings.quote: It will not now be possible to sell assets and buy new, the council will need to retain some or all of the assets for the longer term.

findings.headline: Attempted sale of Chesterford Research Park shareholding attracted interest but no acceptable bid, leaving £88.8m committed to a held asset
findings.detail: In February 2024 the council agreed to market its 50% stake in Chesterford Research Park. Despite significant interest, no acceptable bid was received. The council continues to commit major capital: £68.6m is planned for 2026-2031, with no ability to exit. The asset cannot be sold quickly to meet liquidity needs.
findings.matters: Lenders need to assess the council's actual liquidity position; failure to achieve a sale despite marketing suggests the largest single asset may be harder to realise than expected
findings.figures: 50% share valued at £110.35m; £88.8m in existing loans to subsidiary; £68.6m further investment planned
findings.quote: In February 2024 Council agreed to market, through its wholly owned subsidiary Aspire (CRP) Limited, the 50% share in Chesterford Research Park. Whilst significant interest was shown in the sale process no acceptable bid has to date been received.

findings.headline: The 2026-2031 MTFP contains significant and rising shortfalls which the commercial portfolio can no longer fully offset
findings.detail: The council's original strategy, approved in 2020, was to use commercial property income to cover government funding reductions via a £300m investment fund. Changes to the CIPFA Prudential Code 2021 and MRP rules mean this will no longer work. The council now has no mitigation for forecast shortfalls beyond asset sales, which are discretionary.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand the council's main strategy for bridging budget gaps is no longer viable and there is no named alternative plan
findings.figures: £300m allocation approved; £275.6m deployed; generating £14.8m-£17.7m annual rental income over next five years
findings.quote: the 2026 - 2031 MTFP has significant and rising shortfalls which cannot be fully offset by the income form the commercial portfolio

findings.paper_title: APPENDIX I - UDC PROPOSED 5% REVENUE SAVINGS 2026.27
findings.headline: Health Improvement Grant savings depend on external funding that is not guaranteed
findings.detail: The council proposes a £4k saving in the Health Improvement team budget, intending to 'top up the £4K with the Essex Funding.' However, the document explicitly states: 'The risk is whether this funding pot remains in the future.' This is external funding over which the council has no control.
findings.matters: The council's budget for this service area is now dependent on a funding stream it does not control. If Essex funding is withdrawn, the council faces a pressure it has already assumed away.
findings.figures: £4,000 assumed saving from budget reduction; contingent on continued Essex Funding
findings.quote: There is a ring-fenced health improvement grant from ECC and we are accountable how we spend this. Also we are not sure what we will get next year. So there is the potential to reduce the team budget by £4K and top up the £4K with the Essex Funding. The risk is whether this funding pot remains in the future.

findings.paper_title: APPENDIX I - UDC PROPOSED 5% REVENUE SAVINGS 2026.27
findings.headline: Finance Service training budget cut could create capacity risk if accountant turnover occurs
findings.detail: The council is reducing the finance service training budget by £3.5k and eliminating one of two trainee accountant posts. The document explicitly flags the risk: 'If a current Accountant left and we needed to hire a part qualified replacement with training needs, this would result in a budget pressure.' This suggests the council recognizes its finance function is now at reduced capacity.
findings.matters: A lender depends on the council having finance staff capacity to manage accounts and reporting. Reduced training budget and fewer trainees limits the team's ability to absorb turnover or skill gaps.
findings.figures: £3,500 training reduction; £8,200 professional subscriptions reduction; reduction from 2 trainees to 1
findings.quote: If a current Accountant left and we needed to hire a part qualified replacement with training needs, this would result in a budget pressure.

findings.paper_title: APPENDIX I - UDC PROPOSED 5% REVENUE SAVINGS 2026.27
findings.headline: Original £1.96m savings target only 64% achieved; £700k pushed to 2027/28
findings.detail: The council identified £1.96m in savings targets across all services but allocated only £1.26m to 2026/27, deferring £700k to the following year. Large service areas show zero agreed savings despite targets: Environment (£72.6k target, £0 agreed), Grounds Maintenance (£23.2k target, £0), Street Cleansing (£28.2k), Street Services (£16.6k), Homelessness (£25.1k flagged as 'not possible, see growth bid'), Housing Strategy (£3.4k flagged as 'cannot be reduced').
findings.matters: The council could not find savings it identified as needed, indicating service areas it considers essential or challenging to cut. This suggests budget pressure on those services going forward.
findings.figures: £1,960,430 target; £1,260,430 allocated 2026/27; £700,000 deferred to 2027/28; shortfall of £699,784 (35.7% of target unachieved)
findings.quote: TOTAL SAVINGS IDENTIFIED 1,960,430 / Allocated to 2027/28 700,000 / TOTAL SAVINGS ALLOCATED TO 2026/27 1,536,974 1,260,430

findings.paper_title: APPENDIX I - UDC PROPOSED 5% REVENUE SAVINGS 2026.27
findings.headline: Dunmow Depot sale of £83,750 is conditional on planning permission being granted
findings.detail: The council is claiming £83,750 in savings from disposal of the New Street Depot. This saving is explicitly conditional: 'Sale is subject to planning permission and planning application has been submitted.' If planning is refused, this saving does not happen.
findings.matters: This is an assumed asset realization with material uncertainty. A lender would need to know whether the 2026/27 budget can be met if planning permission is refused.
findings.figures: £83,750 assumed saving; contingent on planning approval
findings.quote: Following sale of New Street Depot. Sale is subject to planning permission and planning application has been submitted.

findings.headline: Contingency budget at 9.9% of funding (£1.735m) due to Blueprint and LGR execution risks
findings.detail: The council's contingency budget is unusually high at 9.9% of total funding. Without Blueprint 2.0 and LGR risks, it would normally be 5.7%. The council is explicitly flagging £500k contingency for Blueprint delivery risk and £250k for LGR cost risk. This high contingency is a material call on the budget if risks crystallise.
findings.matters: High contingency indicates management's lack of confidence in achieving budget targets. If contingency is drawn, the budget deficit worsens immediately.
findings.figures: Total contingency £1.735m (9.9% of funding); Blueprint risk £500k; LGR risk £250k; normal contingency would be 5.7%
findings.quote: The total contingency represents 9.9% of the council's funding, which may seem high, but Blueprint 2.0 and in particular LGR are large risky projects.

findings.headline: HRA transitioning to in-house delivery model (IHDM); significant execution risk on maintenance and repairs
findings.detail: The council is moving HRA maintenance and repairs from external contracts (Axis and UNSL) to in-house delivery model. The budget includes £1.273m additional spend to embed IHDM, deal with legacy issues from the Axis and UNSL contracts, and address new social housing regulations. The council acknowledges: 'There is a risk that the costs to deliver a basic quality of service will be greater than expected or that the transition will not be as smooth, leading to additional costs.'
findings.matters: Contract transitions are high-risk operational changes. Failure to execute efficiently could result in higher-than-budgeted costs or service quality issues in the council's social housing stock.
findings.figures: HRA maintenance and repairs budget increase £1.273m to embed IHDM; new staffing posts created (Insight Officer, Damp/Mould Officer, Complaints Officer)
findings.quote: There is a risk that the costs to deliver a basic quality of service will be greater than expected or that the transition will not be as smooth, leading to additional costs.

findings.headline: Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) grant at risk of £278k reduction; future funding uncertain
findings.detail: DEFRA allocated £1.175m EPR grant for 2026/27, which is £278k less than 2025/26. From 2026/27, this grant must be allocated directly to Refuse and Recycling services to demonstrate use, rather than sitting in general funding. 'The Government has not confirmed this full amount will be maintained, so is a risk for years beyond 2026/27.' Waste and recycling is listed as a high-risk budget area due to market volatility.
findings.matters: EPR funding is not stable. A further reduction would materially impact waste services, which are already subject to fuel and disposal cost volatility.
findings.figures: EPR allocation 2026/27 £1.175m (down £278k from 2025/26); market volatility risk rated High on impact and probability
findings.quote: The Government has not confirmed this full amount will be maintained, so is a risk for years beyond 2026/27.

findings.headline: Housing Benefit Subsidy gap growing £200k per year; Homelessness Prevention Grant severely restricted
findings.detail: The council faces a structural pressure in temporary accommodation: it pays housing benefit to private landlords but receives only a partial government subsidy, creating an annual £200k gap that is growing. From 2026/27, the government's Homelessness Prevention Grant can only be spent 30% on staff salaries, making it much harder to resource homelessness services. The council has put aside additional contingency but notes 'there is no certainty that this is sufficient.'
findings.matters: This is a demand-driven, structural cost that the council cannot control. It will continue to grow as housing costs rise and homelessness increases.
findings.figures: Housing Benefit Subsidy gap growth £200k per year; Homelessness Prevention Grant now 30% for salaries only (down from no restriction)
findings.quote: Housing benefit subsidy gap is growing faster than expected. There is a contingency in Corporate Items but there is no certainty that this is sufficient.

findings.headline: Interest rate exposure of £106m; financing costs consume 75% of net revenue stream
findings.detail: The council holds £106m of short-term borrowing exposed to interest rate movements. Every 0.25% interest rate move costs £250k annually. The Bank of England base rate was cut from 4.0% to 3.75% in December 2025, but the council's treasury advisors forecast rates will stay at 3.25% from mid-2026. Prudential indicator shows financing costs represent 75% of the council's net revenue stream in 2026/27, the highest on record.
findings.matters: Interest rate risk is material and rising. The council's financial sustainability is increasingly dependent on interest rate movements outside its control. High financing costs ratio indicates limited headroom.
findings.figures: £106m short-term borrowing exposure; £250k per 0.25% rate move annually; financing costs 75% of net revenue stream 2026/27
findings.quote: The council is exposed to short-term interest rates to the tune of £106m. Every 0.25% movement in interest rates on £100m is a £250k impact on the council's bottom line over the period of a year.

findings.headline: Commercial property income represents 99% of net revenue stream in 2026/27; Aspire (CRP) is currently up for sale
findings.detail: Investment properties contribute £722k to the 2026/27 budget, mainly from Aspire (CRP) Limited loans and rents from Chesterford Research Park (50% council-owned). The prudential indicator shows net income from commercial investments is 99% of the net revenue stream in 2026/27. However, the document states Aspire 'is currently up for sale'. Loss of this asset would eliminate this income stream and force a major budget rebalancing.
findings.matters: The council is heavily dependent on a single commercial asset that is actively for sale. This represents both immediate income risk and uncertainty about the council's financial position if a sale completes.
findings.figures: Investment Property contribution 2026/27 £722k; commercial income 99% of net revenue stream; borrowing to Aspire £281.4m (Commercial Investments CFR)
findings.quote: subject to the council retaining Aspire (CRP) Limited, as is assumed in the MTFP, although it is currently up for sale.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creates £2m-£3.75m budget uncertainty; council merges 1 April 2028
findings.detail: Uttlesford is merging into a new unitary council on 1 April 2028, creating profound uncertainty over costs, service integration, and future funding levels. The council has set aside £750k over 3 years (2025/26-2027/28) plus a new £2m LGR reserve. However, 'it is difficult to budget for LGR. The council has an annual budget but these are by no means spec'd out and unexpected costs could easily arise.' The contingency budget includes £250k for LGR risk.
findings.matters: LGR is a fundamental structural change affecting the council's viability beyond 2028. Lenders need confidence in the merged entity's financial sustainability and the transition costs.
findings.figures: £750k LGR budget over 3 years; £2m LGR reserve created; £250k contingency for LGR risk; merger date 1 April 2028
findings.quote: It is difficult to budget for LGR. The council has an annual budget but these are by no means spec'd out and unexpected costs could easily arise, whence this sum of money would be called upon.

findings.headline: Blueprint 2.0 savings programme has not identified £6.214m of the £10.024m target needed by 2028/29
findings.detail: The council's Blueprint 2.0 savings programme is critical to managing the FFR impact. Of the £10.024m target across the MTFP, only £2.257m has been applied to 2026/27 and £2.051m identified. This leaves £6.214m 'still to be identified leading into 2028/29'. The council acknowledges: 'Blueprint 2.0 hasn't identified sufficient savings for the final two years as yet. This will need to form part of LGR discussions with merger partners.'
findings.matters: If these savings are not delivered, the council's deficits are understated and reserve depletion accelerates. This is a material execution risk.
findings.figures: Total Blueprint target £10.024m; identified to date £2.257m + £2.051m = £4.308m; gap £6.214m (62%); £8.265m cumulative unallocated by 2030/31
findings.quote: Blueprint 2.0 hasn't identified sufficient savings for the final two years as yet. This will need to form part of LGR discussions with merger partners once known

findings.headline: Usable reserves will be depleted by end of MTFP period; deficits run throughout 5-year plan
findings.detail: The council explicitly states 'usable reserves are all but depleted by the end of the MTFP period' and forecasts cumulative drawdown of reserves of £6.984m by 2030/31. General Fund reserves decline from £23.402m to £17.430m, with further deterioration if Blueprint savings targets are not met. Deficits are planned for every year: £1.630m (2026/27), rising to £2.091m (2029/30).
findings.matters: The council is using reserves to fund current operations, not capital investment. This is unsustainable and a red flag for lending capacity. Reserve depletion reduces financial resilience.
findings.figures: Cumulative reserve drawdown £6.984m over MTFP; General Fund reserve C/fwd 2030/31 £17.430m (down from £23.402m); annual deficits £1.630m, £1.799m, £610m, £2.091m
findings.quote: usable reserves are all but depleted by the end of the MTFP period and, subject to LGR, significant further savings need to be identified in the last years of the current MTFP.

findings.headline: One-year Adjustment Support Grant masks underlying deficit; full FFR impact hits from 2026/27 onwards
findings.detail: The government provided a one-year matching grant of £1.015m to soften FFR impact in 2026/27, but the council assumes this is 'one-year only'. After 2026/27, the full FFR reduction hits unmitigated. Transitional protection also expires after year 3, creating a material funding cliff. Revenue Support Grant collapses from £6.165m in 2026/27 to £2.205m by 2030/31 (64% cut).
findings.matters: The current budget masks a structural deficit. Lenders need to understand the council's plans for years 2-5, when this grant disappears and funding falls dramatically.
findings.figures: RSG falls from £6,165k (2026/27) to £2,205k (2030/31); Adjustment Support Grant £1,015k for 2026/27 only
findings.quote: The Government has mitigated the impact of the reduction in 2026/27 by way of a matching 'Adjustment Support Grant'. At the present time the indications are that this is a one-year only grant and for the purposes of this budget that assumption applies.

findings.headline: Fair Funding Review cuts Uttlesford's funding by 4-5% and the council is in the top 20 worst-affected districts
findings.detail: The government's FFR formula change announced 9 February 2026 reduced Uttlesford's funding by a further £1.015 million annually. Compared to 2024/25, funding falls 4%; compared to 2025/26, it falls 5%. The council notes this 'has particularly hit UDC badly' and Uttlesford appears in the Rural Services Network's top 20 percentile of councils worst affected by FFR.
findings.matters: This is a permanent structural reduction in grant funding, not a temporary pressure. It directly affects the council's revenue base and borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: £1.015m annual reduction (announced 9 February 2026); 4-5% funding reduction versus prior years
findings.quote: This has particularly hit UDC badly as this has led to a reduction in funding of 4% when compared to 2024/25 and 5% when compared to 2025/26

findings.headline: Council must retain PWLB access by declaring commercial investments are not primarily for yield, creating potential tension with capital strategy
findings.detail: New PWLB rules restrict lending to councils buying investment assets primarily for yield. The council explicitly states it will avoid this activity to maintain PWLB access. However, commercial investments make up the majority of the capital programme (£266-314m of £361-419m CFR), creating potential policy constraint.
findings.matters: Loss of PWLB access would force the council to seek more expensive alternative borrowing sources, directly increasing interest costs and reducing affordability
findings.figures: Commercial investments as % of CFR: 74% (2025) → 75% (2029); Current PWLB borrowing: £207m of £294.5m total (70%)
findings.quote: PWLB loans are no longer available to local authorities planning to buy investment assets primarily for yield; the Council intends to avoid this activity in order to retain its access to PWLB loans.

findings.headline: Capital programme requires £378m borrowing over five years, predominantly for commercial investments
findings.detail: The council's Capital Financing Requirement grows from £361m to £419m over the forecast period, driven by capital expenditure that is heavily weighted to commercial investments (£266-314m) rather than core services. The council must borrow £378m in total over the forecast period to fund this.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess the returns on commercial investments and whether the capital programme is sustainable, and whether commercial asset valuations are stable
findings.figures: CFR: £361m (2025) → £419m (2029); Commercial investments within CFR: £266m (2025) → £314m (2029); Total borrowing requirement: £378m over forecast period
findings.quote: The Council has an increasing CFR due to the capital programme, but minimal investments and will therefore be required to borrow up to £378m over the forecast period.

findings.headline: Pension actuarial controls ineffective for second consecutive year; £2.15m minimum funding liability applied
findings.detail: Controls for reviewing the council's defined benefit pension valuation are ineffective for the second year running. Management's review is insufficiently detailed and documented to be relied upon. As a result, a minimum funding liability of £2,150k has been applied to restrict the net pension surplus to nil, reflecting that the surplus cannot be recovered given future service costs and minimum funding requirements.
findings.matters: The pension scheme represents material liabilities (£82.1m) and assets (£119.9m). Without effective review controls on actuarial assumptions, pension valuations could be materially wrong. A persistent, unresolved control weakness (second year) indicates governance risk.
findings.figures: Defined benefit asset £119.9m (up £5.4m YoY); defined benefit liability £82.1m (up £9.3m YoY); minimum funding liability £2,150k
findings.quote: Actuarial assumptions are assessed by management for appropriateness. However, the review was not performed on a sufficiently detailed or documented basis to allow us to rely on the control. Consequently, we concluded that controls in place to review the valuation were ineffective, consistent with the prior period.

findings.headline: Segregation of duties control failure in journal posting system due to General Ledger limitations
findings.detail: The auditor identified a control deficiency in the automated segregation of duties for posting journal transactions. This deficiency arises from limitations in the council's General Ledger system itself, not from process failures. While testing of high-risk journals found no unsupported entries, the underlying control weakness creates an ongoing fraud risk.
findings.matters: Segregation of duties is a foundational control against fraudulent or erroneous transactions. A weakness here increases the risk that management override, unauthorized transactions, or errors could be recorded in the financial statements without detection.
findings.figures: 8 high-risk journal entries examined
findings.quote: We have identified a control deficiency regarding the enforcement of automated segregation of duties in posting of journal transactions due to the limitations of the General Ledger system.

findings.headline: Control deficiencies identified in management review of £590m+ property and investment assets
findings.detail: The auditor has identified control deficiencies in management's review processes for Council Dwellings (£375.8m), Other Land and Buildings (£45.6m), and Investment Property (£170.2m). In each case, management lacks a formal, documented review process for the valuation reports produced by external valuers. This represents a significant gap in internal controls over assets totalling over £590m.
findings.matters: Property and investment assets represent the majority of the council's balance sheet and collateral position. Without formal management review controls, there is elevated risk that valuations could be materially wrong without detection, affecting reported net worth and borrowing covenant compliance.
findings.figures: Council Dwellings £375.8m (£3.9m increase YoY); Other Land & Buildings £45.6m (£1m decrease YoY); Investment Property £170.2m (£3.9m increase YoY); total £590.6m
findings.quote: We evaluated the design and implementation of controls in place for management to review the valuation and the appropriateness of assumptions used and have raised a control deficiency around the lack of formal review of the valuation report.

findings.headline: No audit assurance over usable reserves since 2019-20 due to legacy audit backlog
findings.detail: The auditor states there is no assurance over the level of usable reserves for the six years from 2019-20 onwards. This is a material gap because councils face statutory duty to balance their annual budget, and when they do not, financial pressures fall on usable reserves and constrain the following year's budget. Without verified opening reserves position, it is impossible to assess the council's true financial position or borrowing capacity.
findings.matters: Usable reserves are the only resources a council can freely spend. Without verified reserves since 2019-20, a lender cannot determine available headroom, the council's resilience to cost pressures, or its actual borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: 2019-20 onwards (six financial years)
findings.quote: There is no assurance provided over the level of usable reserves for 2019-20 onwards, therefore there is a risk relating to the accuracy of the opening level of reserves available to the Council to support cost pressures.

findings.headline: Auditors issuing disclaimer of opinion on 2024/25 financial statements due to inability to verify reserves split before statutory backstop date
findings.detail: KPMG cannot obtain sufficient audit evidence over the split of usable and unusable reserves at 31 March 2025 and 31 March 2024 before the statutory backstop date of 27 February 2026. The auditor views this inability as 'pervasive to the Council's and the Group's financial position' and is therefore disclaiming their opinion on the entire 2024/25 financial statements.
findings.matters: A disclaimer of opinion means the council's financial position cannot be independently verified. Lenders cannot reliably assess the council's net worth, solvency, or reserves available to support borrowing and spending commitments.
findings.figures: Statutory backstop date 27 February 2026
findings.quote: we have determined that there is insufficient time to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence over the split of useable and unusable reserves as at 31 March 2025 or 31 March 2024 ahead of the backstop, and, in our view, this is pervasive to the Council's and the Group's financial position

findings.headline: Large capital financing requirement of £357m funded via £315m of borrowing, creating material leverage.
findings.detail: The council has invested significantly in commercial properties across England, including a £357m capital financing requirement as of 31 March 2025. This is partially funded through £198m long-term and £117m short-term borrowing. While the gross debt-to-CFR ratio of 0.54:1 is within prudent limits, the absolute scale of borrowing is substantial for a rural district council.
findings.matters: A lender assessing creditworthiness needs to understand the scale of the council's capital structure; £315m of debt against a usable reserves base of £33m and recurrent budget gaps creates refinancing risk if investment property values decline or income yields disappoint.
findings.figures: Capital financing requirement £357m; long-term borrowings £198m; short-term borrowings £117m; gross debt to CFR ratio 0.54:1
findings.quote: At 31 March 2025, the Council had a capital financing requirement of £357m (see note 38 to the financial statements), reflecting the scale of investments that have been made. This is partly funded through £198m of long-term borrowings and £117m of short-term borrowings held at 31 March 2025.

findings.headline: Housing services contractor terminated mid-contract after non-performance, and replacement contractor also terminated within eight months.
findings.detail: Uttlesford Norse Services Limited (UNSL) was terminated effective 31 March 2025 due to non-performance issues and a prior self-referral to the housing regulator. The council then appointed Axis Europe as replacement but terminated that contract in December 2025 due to performance concerns. This creates a pattern of service continuity risk and suggests governance or commissioning weaknesses.
findings.matters: Repeated contractor failures in a core service (housing repairs and maintenance) indicate either poor contract management, unrealistic expectations, or difficulty attracting capable providers; this affects service delivery and council reputation.
findings.figures: UNSL contract terminated 31 March 2025; Axis Europe contract terminated December 2025 (after 8 months)
findings.quote: the Council reached a mutual agreement to terminate its contract with Norse effective 31 March 2025. We note that the Council has subsequently terminated the contract with Axis in December 2025 due to performance concerns noted from the review of the work completed within the first eight months of the contract.

findings.headline: Council faces a £6.792m annual budget gap from 2026-27 onwards due to loss of external funding.
findings.detail: After identifying that £8.5m of annual efficiencies are needed by 2029 to sustain the council, only £2.5m has been identified as of year-end 2024-25, leaving a £6m shortfall. The council holds sufficient reserves to cover the budget gap over the five-year medium-term financial strategy period, but reliance on reserves for ongoing deficits is not sustainable long-term.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council can balance its budget from operations or is consuming reserves; a £6.792m recurring gap with only £2.5m of the required £8.5m savings identified indicates material execution risk.
findings.figures: £8.5m efficiencies target by 2029; £2.5m identified; £6.792m budget gap per year from 2026-27
findings.quote: the Council needed to identify recurrent efficiencies of approximately £7m target to be achieved by 2028 in order for the general fund balances to be sustainable. In the current year, the Blueprint Uttlesford plan was updated to £8.5m by 2029

findings.headline: Auditors have issued a disclaimer of opinion on the financial statements due to insufficient audit evidence.
findings.detail: KPMG was unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence over Assets under Construction and movements in usable and unusable reserves, and could not verify comparative figures for 2023-24 ahead of the statutory deadline. This means the auditors cannot confirm whether the financial statements give a true and fair view. Any adjustments would affect net assets, reserve splits, and reported income and expenditure.
findings.matters: A disclaimer of opinion signals material uncertainty about the council's reported financial position, creating risk for lenders assessing actual assets, reserves, and solvency.
findings.figures: 31 March 2025 balance sheet cannot be audited; comparative 2023-24 figures also unaudited
findings.quote: We have been unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence over a number of areas of the financial statements as we have been unable to perform the procedures that we consider necessary to form our opinion on the financial statements ahead of the Backstop Date.

findings.paper_title: Appendix J Capital Programme pdf version
findings.headline: Substantial commercial property investment at Chesterford Research Park drives capital programme, with £64.6m committed over five years.
findings.detail: The Investments section accounts for the majority of planned expenditure, dominated by three Chesterford Research Park projects: Building 1100/1200 New Build (£10m–£20m annually), Lease End Units Refurbishment (£1.5m–£3m annually), and Building 500 New Build (£2.5m–£5m in later years). The council's capital spend peaks at £23m in 2027/28, with investments accounting for most of this outlay.
findings.matters: Commercial property investment by a local authority carries vacancy, management, and revenue risk; a lender needs to understand the business case, lease terms, occupancy assumptions, and expected revenue to assess whether the council can service debt from these returns.

findings.headline: Council believes the current short-term borrowing position is untenable given the impending transition to Unitary Authority.
findings.detail: The Motion explicitly calls the position of significant short-term borrowing during the transition to a new Unitary Authority untenable, and proposes either replacing all short-term borrowing with long-term secured borrowing or selling assets to reduce exposure.
findings.matters: Structural reorganisation creates uncertainty about debt liability allocation and financial capacity. Short-term debt during this transition increases the risk of forced refinancing in unfavourable conditions.
findings.figures: none
findings.quote: This risk, coupled with the impending transition to a new Unitary Authority (of whatever nature that may be), that the current position, with a significant proportion of short-term borrowing, is untenable and that this should be rectified by one or both of the following measures

findings.headline: Commercial investment borrowing is not directly secured by the underlying assets.
findings.detail: Although the borrowing is understood to be backed by the value of the investments, the debt is not formally secured against those assets, limiting the council's recourse if the assets underperform or must be liquidated.
findings.matters: Unsecured debt on commercial investments increases the council's legal exposure and complicates recovery if the investments fail to deliver returns or need to be sold.
findings.figures: none
findings.quote: It is understood that the borrowing is backed by the investment, but that borrowing is not directly secured by those assets.

findings.headline: Up to 40% of commercial investment borrowing is on short-term loans, creating significant refinancing risk.
findings.detail: The council is funding almost all commercial investment through borrowing, with a large proportion—up to 40%—taken on short-term terms. This exposes the council to interest rate and roll-over risk.
findings.matters: Refinancing risk on this scale can force rate-taking in adverse markets, as evidenced by the recent doubling in rates, and creates instability during periods of market stress or structural change.
findings.figures: up to 40%
findings.quote: Whilst it is the case that almost all of the commercial investment by this council is funded by borrowing it is evident that a large proportion of the borrowing (up to 40%) is on short-term loans.

findings.headline: Replacement short-term borrowing costs almost twice the original rate after two-month loan matured.
findings.detail: Original borrowing for Chesterford Research Park was approved at 3.99% on a two-month term in August 2025. That loan has now been repaid and replacement borrowing is at an interest rate of almost twice that figure, representing a material increase in financing costs.
findings.matters: A doubling of borrowing costs signals either adverse market conditions or changed credit assessment, and materially worsens the economics of the underlying investment.
findings.figures: 3.99%, almost twice the original figure
findings.quote: It was stated at that meeting that the additional borrowing would be at a rate of 3.99%. However, that loan had a term of just two months and has now been repaid. The replacement borrowing is at an interest rate of almost twice the original figure.

findings.headline: Induction health and safety training ownership is unclear and monitoring has lapsed
findings.detail: A 2022/23 audit recommendation to centralize monitoring of mandatory induction training was transferred from HR to the Health and Safety operational team in April 2023. However, the teams have different understandings of what responsibilities were transferred, and the HR induction tracker has not been updated. The Health and Safety Officer has been on long-term absence, preventing access to the central database and leaving the council unable to confirm whether all new staff completed mandatory induction training.
findings.matters: The council cannot evidence that all staff received mandatory health and safety induction training and is therefore unable to defend itself on its duty of care in the event of a health and safety incident.
findings.figures: Recommendation from 2022/23 audit; responsibility transferred April 2023; still unresolved
findings.quote: there is no monitoring and record-keeping of induction training to evidence that mandatory training courses have been provided and completed

findings.headline: External fire risk assessments completed but recommendations remain untracked and unimplemented
findings.detail: External fire risk assessments identified recommendations for Little Canfield, London Road Offices, Vehicle workshop, and Walpole Offices, but the audit found no mechanism in place to track progress of these recommendations or document completion. Additionally, fire evacuation procedures for other buildings remain incomplete, and there is no available list of nominated fire marshals or their training records.
findings.matters: Unimplemented fire safety recommendations create ongoing liability exposure and represent a failure in management follow-through on audit recommendations; these affect occupant safety and regulatory compliance.
findings.figures: External fire risk assessments completed for 4 locations; all high-priority recommendations target December 2025 for completion
findings.quote: there is no evidence that mechanism is in place to track the progress of th ese recommendations that may be work in progress

findings.headline: Internal audit opinion is LIMITED ASSURANCE due to significant control weaknesses in health and safety
findings.detail: The 2024/25 audit of Corporate Health and Safety assigned LIMITED ASSURANCE, indicating significant control weaknesses that could put achievement of key service objectives at risk and result in error, fraud, loss or reputational damage. Four high-priority findings were identified, two at medium priority, and one at low priority.
findings.matters: A limited assurance audit opinion signals admitted weaknesses in the council's governance environment; lending decisions account for whether control weaknesses in critical compliance areas indicate broader systemic risks.
findings.figures: 4 high priority findings, 2 medium priority findings, 1 low priority finding
findings.quote: LIMITED ASSURANCE

findings.headline: Recovery to reliable audit assurance will extend multiple years due to insufficient evidence
findings.detail: KPMG determined there was insufficient time before the February 2025 backstop to complete the 2023/24 audit with proper evidence. Rebuilding assurance work must be phased over multiple audit years. Success depends on the council's ability to locate underlying transaction records and corporate knowledge from the disclaimed periods.
findings.matters: The need to phase rebuilding over years, contingent on locating historical records, suggests the council may lack adequate financial documentation or controls. This extends the period during which independent audit assurance is unavailable.
findings.figures: Illustrative pathway: Disclaimer (2023/24) → Disclaimer/Qualified (2024/25) → Qualified (2025/26) → Unmodified (2026/27)
findings.quote: We concluded there was insufficient time before the February 2025 backstop to complete our audit to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence

findings.headline: Audit opinions disclaimed for five years; 2024/25 likely to receive another disclaimer
findings.detail: Previous auditors issued disclaimed audit opinions for four financial years through 2022/23. KPMG disclaimed 2023/24 on 28 February 2025. Because opening balances and prior-year comparatives remain impacted by these disclaimers, the 2024/25 audit is likely to be disclaimed again.
findings.matters: A disclaimed audit opinion means the auditor cannot provide assurance that financial statements are free from material and pervasive misstatement. Multiple consecutive years of disclaimers leave creditors unable to verify the council's true financial position.
findings.figures: Five consecutive financial years: four through 2022/23 (previous auditors), plus 2023/24 (KPMG), plus 2024/25 (likely)
findings.quote: our audit opinion is likely to be disclaimed again in 2024/25

findings.headline: Social Housing Decarbonisation Grant audit identified provider contractual issues, requiring scope to be changed to a lessons-learned review rather than standard compliance testing.
findings.detail: During preliminary work, the audit team identified contractual issues with the Social Housing Decarbonisation Grant provider that required resolution. The grant was prioritised for review due to its complexity, value and time-sensitive delivery requirements. The audit scope was rescoped to review how the council reached the current position and identify lessons for future grant delivery.
findings.matters: Issues with external grant delivery on time-sensitive environmental funding could result in clawback of unspent money, failure to deliver expected outputs, or reduced funding access, affecting both HRA sustainability and council financial planning.
findings.figures: No value disclosed; flagged as significant due to complexity and time pressures
findings.quote: The Social Housing Decarbonisation grant was prioritised due to its complexity, value, and the time pressures associated with delivery. As work was starting on the audit, we discovered that there were contractual issues with the provider that were being resolved. It became clear that better value would be attained if the audit were rescoped to focus on how we reached the current situation and what lessons can be learnt for the future.

findings.headline: Internal audit plan delivery running at 13% against 90% and 75% targets for March and April respectively, due to staff absences and competing service demands.
findings.detail: The council's audit function is significantly behind schedule. Only 13% of audits have reached draft report stage, well below the 90% target for March 2026. Delays are attributed to staff availability affected by absences and competing demands, plus the rescoping of the External Funding/Grants Received audit.
findings.matters: Slow audit delivery reduces internal oversight of council operations and controls, delays identification of control failures and remediation tracking, creating a governance gap that extends through a period of system change and financial pressure.
findings.figures: 13% actual delivery vs 90% target for draft reports by March; 13% vs 75% target for final reports by April
findings.quote: Audit Plan delivered to Draft Report Stage by 31st March: 90% 13%; Audit Plan delivered to final report stage by 30th April: 75% 13%. The commencement of the 2025/26 audit plan has been slower than originally scheduled, due to a combination of operational factors. Staff availability has been affected by a mix of absences and competing service demands

findings.headline: Housing rent arrears grew by £62,148 to £640,665 as of June 2025, up from £578,517 in January 2024, with staffing restructure underway to address collection.
findings.detail: The council is implementing a high priority audit recommendation to address housing management and rent collection through staff restructuring and recruitment to clear a backlog of rent arrears. The Director of Finance has been formally briefed on the arrears position, which represents a material increase over 18 months.
findings.matters: Growing housing arrears represent a direct loss of HRA revenue and indicate collection problems that could pressure housing revenue account finances, require increased doubtful debt provisions, and affect borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: £640,665 (29 June 2025) versus £578,517 (January 2024); increase of £62,148 or 10.7%
findings.quote: On 29 June 2025, total rent arrears was £640,665 (compared to £578,517 in January 2024). The Strategic Director of Housing Health and Communities has raised this with the Director of Finance Revenues and Benefits.

findings.headline: Uttlesford had 27 audit recommendations overdue as of 1 August 2025, including 9 rated High severity.
findings.detail: The recommendation tracker shows 27 overdue recommendations distributed across 9 High severity, 17 Medium severity, and 1 Low severity items. Of 72 total recommendations being tracked for 2025-26, 19 had been closed by that date. The existence of High severity recommendations remaining unimplemented beyond their due date indicates governance or operational control weaknesses the council has not yet addressed.
findings.matters: Lenders evaluate governance quality and the council's track record of implementing control improvements as creditworthiness indicators; overdue audit recommendations suggest operational failings and inability to remediate control weaknesses within expected timescales.
findings.figures: 27 overdue recommendations (9 High, 17 Medium, 1 Low); 72 total tracked in 2025-26; 19 closed by 1 August 2025
findings.quote: Overdue recommendations 1 August 2025

findings.headline: Finance team capacity previously constrained, causing late accounts publication; now strengthened with new qualified recruits publishing 2024/25 accounts ahead of deadline.
findings.detail: Prior year CIPFA review identified capacity constraints and single points of failure in the finance function. Draft 2023/24 accounts were published 15 January 2025, several months after the statutory 31 May 2024 deadline. Council has since recruited new qualified accountants from outside and promoted internal employees with recent accounting qualifications, enabling publication of draft 2024/25 accounts ahead of the statutory deadline.
findings.matters: Late accounts indicate prior control environment weaknesses; improved timeliness and team capacity now provide better financial visibility and reduced single-point-of-failure risk.
findings.figures: 15 January 2025 (late deadline), 31 May 2024 (statutory deadline), 31/05/2025 (target met)
findings.quote: The draft 2023/24 accounts were published for inspection on 15 January 2025, several months after the statutory deadline of 31 May 2024.

findings.headline: Housing services contract with Norse terminated after non-performance; new contractor Axis Europe starts April 2025 following regulator involvement.
findings.detail: Council terminated its contract with Uttlesford Norse Services Limited (UNSL) effective 31 March 2025 after multiple non-performance issues. UNSL self-referred to the regulator of social housing in 2021 (referral closed 2023 after additional oversight), and a follow-up internal audit in 2024 resulted in limited assurance rating. New contractor Axis Europe has been appointed for 2025/26 after housing stock condition surveys by Savil.
findings.matters: Service transition creates operational continuity risk; prior regulator involvement and limited assurance rating indicate prior control weaknesses in this critical service area.
findings.quote: During the service contract period, several non-performance issues were identified. This resulted in a self-referral to the regulator of social housing in 2021, which was subsequently closed in 2023 following the implementation of additional oversight and monitoring. In 2024, a follow up internal audit was undertaken which resulted in a limited assurance rating.

findings.headline: Council holds £357 million capital financing requirement funded through £198m long-term and £117m short-term borrowings to support commercial property investments.
findings.detail: The council has made significant investments in commercial properties across England, including a joint venture stake in Chesterford Park research park, to generate income supporting the underlying cost base. This investment strategy has resulted in a substantial borrowing position with £198m long-term borrowings and £117m short-term borrowings as at 31 March 2025. The council is exploring using capital receipts to reduce borrowing.
findings.matters: The scale of short-term borrowing (£117m) creates refinancing risk, and the dependency on commercial property income to support operational costs introduces market and asset performance risks.
findings.figures: £357m capital financing requirement, £198m long-term borrowings, £117m short-term borrowings
findings.quote: The Council's investment property portfolio consists of seven properties, including an investment in Chesterford Park research park, which is managed through a joint venture vehicle held within the Council's Aspire CRP subsidiary.

findings.headline: Council has identified only £2.5m of the £8.5m annual efficiencies needed by 2029, facing £6.5m annual funding gap from 2026/27.
findings.detail: The council updated its efficiency target to £8.5m by 2029 due to inflation, service investments and external factors. To date only £2.5m has been identified, leaving a £6.5m annual shortfall from 2026/27 due to loss of external funding. The council holds sufficient reserves to cover this gap over the five-year MTFS period, but execution risk on the remaining £6m remains significant.
findings.matters: A lender would be concerned about the large gap between identified and required savings, and the heavy reliance on reserve depletion to manage funding shortfalls.
findings.figures: £8.5m by 2029, £2.5m identified, £6.5 million per year from 2026/27
findings.quote: To date the Council has identified £2.5m of the £8.5m of annual efficiencies that are required in order to achieve financial balance over the life of the five year strategy.

findings.headline: Digital Innovation & Commercialisation overspent by £511k, the only significant service overspend in the general fund
findings.detail: Against a budget of £3.334m, Digital Innovation & Commercialisation spent £3.845m, a 15% overspend of £511k. This is the single largest variance across general fund services, standing alone as the only area with substantial positive variance while all others underspent.
findings.matters: Service overspends indicate potential cost control or project governance weakness; digital initiatives are especially prone to scope creep, and this sustained overspend in a discretionary area suggests issues that may extend to other budget management
findings.figures: Budget £3,334k, outturn £3,845k, overspend £511k
findings.quote: Digital Innovation & Commercialisation 3,334 3,845 511

findings.headline: HRA new builds capital investment slipped 61%, delivering only £885k of £2.315m budget
findings.detail: The HRA spent £885k on new builds against a budget of £2.315m, leaving £1.430m unspent. This represents a 61% variance in planned housing construction and suggests significant delays or scaling back of new housing schemes. The unspent amount is being held in earmarked HRA reserves to fund slipped projects in future years.
findings.matters: Housing delivery is central to HRA sustainability; capital slippage this substantial signals either project delays or delivery obstacles that affect the council's ability to execute its housing strategy and demonstrate execution capability to lenders
findings.figures: New builds: budget £2,315k, outturn £885k, shortfall £1,430k

findings.paper_title: REPORT - Provisional Outturn 2024.25 - Appendix E (For Cabinet)
findings.headline: Credit quality of investment portfolio declined slightly, with bail-in exposure rising from 29% to 47% year-on-year
findings.detail: The council's treasury investment portfolio credit score fell from 5.46 to 5.38 (both A+ rated), and more significantly, exposure to bail-in risk (where creditors can lose deposits in bank stress scenarios) rose from 29% to 47%. Weighted average maturity of investments lengthened from 96 days to 171 days. This reflects the council holding more capital with fewer banks and holding it longer.
findings.matters: Rising bail-in exposure means a larger proportion of the council's cash is at risk in a banking stress scenario. The investment portfolio is the council's liquid buffer against cash flow volatility.
findings.figures: Credit score 5.46 to 5.38 (both A+), bail-in exposure 29% to 47%, weighted average maturity 96 to 171 days

findings.paper_title: REPORT - Provisional Outturn 2024.25 - Appendix E (For Cabinet)
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account capital spend significantly underran budget at £5.197m actual against £9.190m budget (44% underspend)
findings.detail: The HRA capital programme delivered only £5.197m of planned £9.190m spending (underspend of £3.993m, or 43%). This is material underdelivery of housing capital investment. The General Fund overran slightly (£5.015m vs £4.906m budget), but commercial investments also overran (£14.750m vs £13.732m budget by £1.018m), suggesting capital constraints may have affected housing delivery.
findings.matters: Significant underspend in HRA capital signals either delivery challenges in the housing programme or forecasting weakness, both of which affect the council's capacity to generate housing income and service HRA debt.
findings.figures: HRA budget £9.190m, actual £5.197m, underspend £3.993m (43%)
findings.quote: Housing Revenue Account 9,190 5,197 (3,993)

findings.paper_title: REPORT - Provisional Outturn 2024.25 - Appendix E (For Cabinet)
findings.headline: Council's net borrowing of £313.6m far exceeds cash investments of £15.2m, leaving exposure to refinancing risk as 10-year PWLB rates rose from 4.74% to 5.42% during the year
findings.detail: Uttlesford is a net borrower with £313.6m in loans and only £15.2m in treasury investments (predominantly money market funds and local authority deposits). The report explicitly states: 'the Council remains exposed to interest rate risk on refinancing.' During 2024/25, 10-year PWLB rates rose from 4.74% to 5.42% (68 basis points). The council's weighted average borrowing cost is 4.52%, with short-term borrowing at 5.37% (where the council holds £97.5m of the total). Refinancing at the year-end rate environment would cost materially more.
findings.matters: The gap between borrowing and investments exposes the council to rising interest costs if rates stay elevated when loans mature. Short-term borrowing at 5.37% signals reliance on roll-over funding in a volatile rate environment.
findings.figures: £313.6m borrowing vs £15.2m investments (net £298.4m), 10-year PWLB 4.74% to 5.42%, short-term borrowing 5.37%, weighted average cost 4.52%
findings.quote: However, the Council's borrowing far exceeds the balances invested, and the Council remains exposed to interest rate risk on refinancing.

findings.paper_title: REPORT - Provisional Outturn 2024.25 - Appendix E (For Cabinet)
findings.headline: Council holds £250.8m in commercial investments and explicitly states it will review exit options before borrowing further
findings.detail: Uttlesford holds £171.2m in directly owned investment properties and £79.6m in long-term loans to its subsidiary Aspire (which holds 50% stake in Chesterford Research Park). These investments generated £10.4m in net income in 2024/25 (5.3% return on the property holdings alone). The council notes that under the 2021 CIPFA Prudential Code it cannot borrow to invest primarily for financial return, and explicitly states: 'Before undertaking further additional borrowing the Authority will review the options for exiting these investments.'
findings.matters: The scale of commercial investment (£250.8m) relative to total net borrowing (£298.4m) means the council's capital structure is heavily dependent on commercial asset valuations and rental income. The statement about reviewing exit options signals pressure on the borrowing model.
findings.figures: £250.8m total commercial investments, £171.2m investment properties, £79.6m shareholding loans, £10.4m net income in 2024/25
findings.quote: The Authority currently holds £250.8m in commercial investments primarily for financial return that were purchased prior to the change in the CIPFA Prudential Code. This includes £171.2m in investment properties and £79.6m in long term investments in a shareholding company. Before undertaking further additional borrowing the Authority will review the options for exiting these investments.

findings.paper_title: REPORT - Provisional Outturn 2024.25 - Appendix E (For Cabinet)
findings.headline: Council refinanced Phoenix Life loan at 4.925% average rate, up from 2.86% on the loan being repaid
findings.detail: The council repaid a £35.471m Phoenix Life loan using £25.192m principal plus discount, refinancing into PWLB loans at substantially higher rates. The replacement loans average 4.925% over 5 years versus 2.86% on the original. Despite a £97k arrangement fee, the council reports a saving of approximately £700k in 2024/25 after accounting for new borrowing costs, but this is a one-off benefit. The ongoing annual interest cost is higher until rates fall enough to refinance again.
findings.matters: This shows the council is exposed to refinancing risk, and locks in higher costs for incoming debt. The timing and rate environment matter significantly to borrowing costs.
findings.figures: £35.471m loan repaid, £25.192m (£10.279m discount) refinanced, replacement rates average 4.925% for 5 years vs 2.86% original, £97k fee, £700k 2024/25 saving
findings.quote: As per local government General Fund regulations, this discount is spread over 10 years. The current annuity loan is at 2.86% and the replacement loans averaged 4.925% for an average of 5 years. Therefore, in short term, the annual interest cost will be higher till it can be refinanced when interest rates are lower.

news_drafts.headline: Transport operations audit found six operational categories unsatisfactory; remediation due July 2026
news_drafts.lead: Operational compliance failures in transport operations represent control weaknesses and potential licence liability. Tight remediation timelines suggest urgent issues that could affect service continuity.

news_drafts.headline: Social Housing Regulator gave C2 rating (below target C1), requiring improvement in tenant engagement and repairs
news_drafts.lead: A C2 regulatory rating indicates the council is not fully meeting regulatory expectations in housing management and service delivery. This directly reflects on the quality and compliance of housing operations.

news_drafts.headline: Information governance reporting has fallen behind due to resourcing constraints, with backlog extending into 2026/27
news_drafts.lead: Information governance is a statutory reporting requirement. Persistent resourcing gaps preventing compliance reports suggest staff constraints and inability to adequately manage data protection and compliance risks.
